query.original_query: language complexity syntax effect on LLM reasoning and in-context learning

sub_queries.semantic_query: how syntactic complexity and linguistic structure affect reasoning and in-context learning in large language models, probing attention heads and circuits for syntax processing during few-shot prompting
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate how syntactic complexity modulates reasoning and in-context learning in large language models by probing attention heads and circuits during few-shot prompting. Using causal tracing and activation patching, we analyze the role of specific attention heads in processing hierarchical syntactic structures, such as nested clauses and long-distance dependencies, during chain-of-thought and few-shot tasks. Our analysis reveals that attention heads in middle and late layers exhibit specialized responses to syntactic perturbations, with distinct circuits recruited for processing subject-verb agreement and relative clause embeddings. We find that disrupting these syntactic circuits via activation patching significantly degrades in-context learning performance, particularly for tasks requiring compositional reasoning. Results show that syntactic structure is encoded in a distributed manner across multiple attention heads, with some heads acting as syntactic "hubs" that integrate information from earlier layers. The findings suggest that syntactic processing is not merely a precursor to semantic reasoning but is deeply intertwined with the mechanisms underlying few-shot generalization.

sub_queries.semantic_query: influence of syntactic complexity on human sentence processing and reasoning, garden path effects, relative clause processing, working memory load during comprehension of complex syntax
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigated the influence of syntactic complexity on real-time sentence processing and subsequent reasoning accuracy. Participants read sentences containing subject- and object-extracted relative clauses, varying in embedding depth, while undergoing self-paced reading. We measured reading times at the critical verb region and administered a post-trial verification task to assess comprehension. Results indicate that object-extracted relative clauses, particularly those with center-embedded structures, elicited significantly longer reading times compared to subject-extracted counterparts, consistent with increased working memory load during syntactic integration. Furthermore, accuracy on reasoning questions was reduced following complex syntactic structures, suggesting that processing difficulty cascades into higher-level semantic interpretation. Findings support the hypothesis that garden path effects and relative clause processing difficulty are modulated by the availability of working memory resources, with implications for models of sentence comprehension that posit a limited-capacity parser. These results align with prior work on the role of syntactic complexity in modulating cognitive load during language comprehension.

papers.title: Identifying Semantic Induction Heads to Understand In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether attention heads in transformers encode semantic relationships (syntactic dependencies and knowledge graph relations) and how the formation of such semantic induction heads correlates with the emergence of in-context learning abilities.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers semantic induction heads in transformers that encode semantic relationships and shows their emergence correlates with the development of in-context learning abilities.
papers.conclusion: The study of semantic induction heads advances understanding of attention head operations and provides insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in transformers encode syntactic dependencies (subj, obj, mod) and semantic relationships from knowledge graphs.
The model's ability to understand dependencies is reflected in attention heads, with some heads specializing in specific relations.
In-context learning emerges progressively in three levels: loss reduction, format compliance, and pattern discovery.
The formation of semantic induction heads coincides with the emergence of pattern discovery in ICL.
Semantic induction heads are crucial for the model's ability to perform in-context learning.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, the lack of transparency in their inference logic raises concerns about their trustworthiness. To gain a better understanding of LLMs, we conduct a detailed analysis of the operations of attention heads and aim to better understand the in-context learning of LLMs. Specifically, we investigate whether attention heads encode two types of relationships between tokens present in natural languages: the syntactic dependency parsed from sentences and the relation within knowledge graphs. We find that certain attention heads exhibit a pattern where, when attending to head tokens, they recall tail tokens and increase the output logits of those tail tokens. More crucially, the formulation of such semantic induction heads has a close correlation with the emergence of the in-context learning ability of language models. The study of semantic attention heads advances our understanding of the intricate operations of attention heads in transformers, and further provides new insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.

papers.title: Induction Heads as an Essential Mechanism for Pattern Matching in In-context Learning
papers.research_question: What is the role of induction heads in few-shot in-context learning? Are they essential for pattern matching in ICL?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that induction heads are essential for few-shot in-context learning, as their ablation leads to significant performance drops in both abstract pattern recognition and NLP tasks.
papers.conclusion: The ablation of induction heads affects few-shot performance more severely than zero-shot performance, and induction heads are a fundamental mechanism underlying ICL.
papers.key_findings:
Ablation of 1% of induction heads leads to substantial ICL performance decreases (up to ~32% for abstract pattern recognition tasks).
For NLP tasks, ablation of induction heads reduces the model's ability to benefit from examples, bringing few-shot performance close to zero-shot.
Attention knockout experiments show that blocking the induction pattern causes performance drops comparable to full head ablations, confirming the specific role of the prefix matching and copying mechanism.
The effects are consistent across two models (Llama-3-8B and InternLM2-20B).
Induction heads utilize a 'fuzzy' version of prefix matching and copying for pattern matching.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on prefix-matching scores as a proxy for induction heads without mechanistic verification.
Attention knockout experiments are confined to abstract-pattern recognition tasks, not verified across NLP tasks.
The experiments do not test whether induction heads are the only computational process contributing to ICL.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown a remarkable ability to learn and perform complex tasks through in-context learning (ICL).However, a comprehensive understanding of its internal mechanisms is still lacking.This paper explores the role of induction heads in a fewshot ICL setting.We analyse two state-of-theart models, Llama-3-8B and InternLM2-20B on abstract pattern recognition and NLP tasks.Our results show that even a minimal ablation of induction heads leads to ICL performance decreases of up to ~32% for abstract pattern recognition tasks, bringing the performance close to random.For NLP tasks, this ablation substantially decreases the model's ability to benefit from examples, bringing few-shot ICL performance close to that of zero-shot prompts.We further use attention knockout to disable specific induction patterns, and present finegrained evidence for the role that the induction mechanism plays in ICL.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: The study finds that a large fraction of attention heads (~70%) and feed-forward networks (~20%) in a 66B parameter language model can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning performance, and that induction heads (capable of primitive operations) overlap with task-important heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, opening up questions on how to pre-train them to more effectively perform in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 70% of attention heads can be removed with minimal decline in task performance across 14 NLP tasks.
Approximately 20% of feed-forward networks can be removed with minimal decline in task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in intermediate layers, while important FFNs are in later layers.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples.
Induction heads (heads scoring highly on prefix matching and copying) overlap with task-specific important heads, suggesting they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
future_direction: Investigating how to pre-train language models to more effectively perform in-context learning.
papers.abstract: Language models have been shown to perform better with an increase in scale on a wide variety of tasks via the in-context learning paradigm. In this paper, we investigate the hypothesis that the ability of a large language model to in-context learn-perform a task is not uniformly spread across all of its underlying components. Using a 66 billion parameter language model (OPT-66B) across a diverse set of 14 downstream tasks, we find this is indeed the case: $\sim$70% of attention heads and $\sim$20% of feed forward networks can be removed with minimal decline in task performance. We find substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples. We also address our hypothesis through a task-agnostic lens, finding that a small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on their ability to perform primitive induction operations associated with in-context learning, namely, prefix matching and copying. These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, reinforcing arguments by Olsson et al. (arXiv:2209.11895) regarding induction head generality to more sophisticated behaviors associated with in-context learning. Overall, our study provides several insights that indicate large language models may be under-trained for in-context learning and opens up questions on how to pre-train language models to more effectively perform in-context learning.

papers.title: Understanding and Controlling Repetition Neurons and Induction Heads in In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between repetition neurons and induction heads in in-context learning, and how does their ablation affect ICL performance and repetitive generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a layer-wise analysis showing that repetition neurons in late layers are critical for ICL, while middle-layer neurons can be ablated to reduce repetition without harming ICL, and proposes a three-segment ablation strategy for this purpose.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that repetition neurons and induction heads form a cascade for pattern recognition in ICL, and that selective ablation of middle-layer repetition neurons can reduce repetitive generation while preserving ICL performance.
papers.key_findings:
The impact of repetition neuron ablation on ICL performance varies significantly with layer depth.
Repetition neurons in output-side layers serve as critical executors of pattern-based predictions, with effects on ICL performance comparable to induction heads.
Joint ablation of both repetition neurons and induction heads leads to a near-complete breakdown of pattern recognition.
Selectively deactivating repetition neurons in middle layers reduces repetition while preserving ICL performance.
future_direction: Generalizing the three-step pipeline (behavioral pattern detection, neuron/head ranking, targeted ablation) to other problems like memorization.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between large language models' (LLMs) ability to recognize repetitive input patterns and their performance on in-context learning (ICL). In contrast to prior work that has primarily focused on attention heads, we examine this relationship from the perspective of skill neurons, specifically repetition neurons. Our experiments reveal that the impact of these neurons on ICL performance varies depending on the depth of the layer in which they reside. By comparing the effects of repetition neurons and induction heads, we further identify strategies for reducing repetitive outputs while maintaining strong ICL capabilities.

papers.title: Which Attention Heads Matter for In-Context Learning?
papers.research_question: Which attention heads (induction heads or function vector heads) are more important for in-context learning in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Function vector (FV) heads are the primary drivers of few-shot in-context learning performance, especially in larger models, and many FV heads evolve from induction heads during training.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that function vector heads are crucial for in-context learning, challenging the prevailing view that induction heads are the key mechanism, and highlights methodological insights for interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
FV heads are more important for few-shot ICL than induction heads, especially in larger models.
Induction heads and FV heads are distinct but correlated.
Many FV heads start as induction heads during training and then transition to the FV mechanism.
The choice of metric (few-shot accuracy vs. token-loss difference) leads to different conclusions about the importance of induction heads.
The relative importance of FV heads increases with model scale.
future_direction: Investigate why induction heads might be necessary precursors to FV heads.
Determine the role of remaining induction heads in fully trained models.
Explore additional mechanisms that could explain ICL capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive in-context learning (ICL) capability, enabling them to perform new tasks using only a few demonstrations in the prompt. Two different mechanisms have been proposed to explain ICL: induction heads that find and copy relevant tokens, and function vector (FV) heads whose activations compute a latent encoding of the ICL task. To better understand which of the two distinct mechanisms drives ICL, we study and compare induction heads and FV heads in 12 language models. Through detailed ablations, we discover that few-shot ICL performance depends primarily on FV heads, especially in larger models. In addition, we uncover that FV and induction heads are connected: many FV heads start as induction heads during training before transitioning to the FV mechanism. This leads us to speculate that induction facilitates learning the more complex FV mechanism that ultimately drives ICL.

papers.title: Decoding In-Context Learning: Neuroscience-inspired Analysis of Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context learning, and how do these changes mediate improvement in behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired framework using Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Attention Ratio Analysis (ARA) to show that in-context learning improves task-critical representations and attention allocation, which correlate with behavioral gains.
papers.conclusion: ICL improves task-critical representations and attention allocation to relevant content in the prompt, and these representational changes are correlated with behavioral gains.
papers.key_findings:
ICL leads to changes in prompt embedding similarity matrices to better encode task-critical information, which in turn improves behavior.
ICL increases the decodability of task-critical information (e.g., line slope) from embeddings via probing classifiers.
ICL shifts attention to relevant content in the prompt (increased attention ratio to informative parts), which correlates with behavioral improvement.
These representational changes are consistent across multiple layers (except the first) in both Llama-2 and Vicuna models.
The proposed methods (RSA and ARA) provide scalable tools for analyzing latent representations in large language models.
future_direction: Study the effects of ICL on improving planning behavior in LLMs by analyzing latent representations before and after ICL in planning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable performance improvement through in-context learning (ICL) by leveraging task-specific examples in the input. However, the mechanisms behind this improvement remain elusive. In this work, we investigate how LLM embeddings and attention representations change following in-context-learning, and how these changes mediate improvement in behavior. We employ neuroscience-inspired techniques such as representational similarity analysis (RSA) and propose novel methods for parameterized probing and measuring ratio of attention to relevant vs. irrelevant information in Llama-2 70B and Vicuna 13B. We designed two tasks with a priori relationships among their conditions: linear regression and reading comprehension. We formed hypotheses about expected similarities in task representations and measured hypothesis alignment of LLM representations before and after ICL as well as changes in attention. Our analyses revealed a meaningful correlation between improvements in behavior after ICL and changes in both embeddings and attention weights across LLM layers. This empirical framework empowers a nuanced understanding of how latent representations shape LLM behavior, offering valuable tools and insights for future research and practical applications.

papers.title: A circuit for predicting hierarchical structure in-context in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether induction heads in LLMs can support in-context learning of complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical dependencies, and how these induction heads themselves learn in-context.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs use adaptive induction heads that learn to attend to correct successor tokens in hierarchical contexts, supported by context matching heads that encode latent contexts, providing a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that LLMs use adaptive induction heads and context matching heads to learn hierarchical dependencies in-context, offering a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads in LLMs can learn to attend to correct successor tokens in-context for sequences with hierarchical dependencies.
Adaptive induction heads are located in later layers, while static induction heads are in earlier layers.
Ablating induction heads severely reduces prediction accuracy, showing their causal role in in-context learning.
Context matching heads encode latent chunk identities and are causally involved in enabling induction heads to learn.
The proposed circuit of context matching heads feeding into induction heads explains hierarchical in-context learning, including in natural language ambiguous cases.
papers.limitation:
The study has not explored other types of in-context learning, such as abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
All learning analyzed happens non-verbally, without explicit verbal reasoning or deliberation.
future_direction: Study induction head behavior in abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
Study induction head behavior in settings with verbal reasoning and deliberation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at in-context learning, the ability to use information provided as context to improve prediction of future tokens. Induction heads have been argued to play a crucial role for in-context learning in Transformer Language Models. These attention heads make a token attend to successors of past occurrences of the same token in the input. This basic mechanism supports LLMs' ability to copy and predict repeating patterns. However, it is unclear if this same mechanism can support in-context learning of more complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical structure. Natural language is teeming with such cases: The article "the" in English usually prefaces multiple nouns in a text. When predicting which token succeeds a particular instance of "the", we need to integrate further contextual cues from the text to predict the correct noun. If induction heads naively attend to all past instances of successor tokens of "the" in a context-independent manner, they cannot support this level of contextual information integration. In this study, we design a synthetic in-context learning task, where tokens are repeated with hierarchical dependencies. Here, attending uniformly to all successor tokens is not sufficient to accurately predict future tokens. Evaluating a range of LLMs on these token sequences and natural language analogues, we find adaptive induction heads that support prediction by learning what to attend to in-context. Next, we investigate how induction heads themselves learn in-context. We find evidence that learning is supported by attention heads that uncover a set of latent contexts, determining the different token transition relationships. Overall, we not only show that LLMs have induction heads that learn, but offer a complete mechanistic account of how LLMs learn to predict higher-order repetitive patterns in-context.

papers.title: How Syntax Specialization Emerges in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does syntactic specialization emerge and evolve over training, and how do model initialization, scale, and training data shape this development?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Syntactic Sensitivity Index (SSI) to measure syntactic specialization in language models, revealing that syntactic sensitivity emerges gradually, concentrates in specific layers, exhibits a critical period, and is consistent across architectures but implemented by different neurons.
papers.conclusion: Provides the first systematic, mechanistic account of how syntactic specialization emerges in transformer language models by introducing SSI and applying it across training trajectories, seeds, and model scales, offering an integrated picture of when, where, and how syntax is represented.
papers.key_findings:
SSI correlates with grammaticality judgment accuracy and outperforms supervised probing methods like SVM and regression.
Syntactic specialization emerges gradually during training, with different syntactic phenomena showing distinct acquisition timelines and layer profiles.
There is a critical period (around 16 million tokens) during which syntactic specialization rapidly emerges and then stabilizes.
While layer-level syntactic representations converge across different random seeds, the specific neurons responsible for syntax sensitivity differ (convergent layers, divergent neurons).
Larger models and more training data enhance syntactic abstraction and specialization, but the effect varies across syntactic phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Relies on sentence embeddings (mean pooling) which may miss token-level nuance or positional dynamics.
BLiMP focuses on binary acceptability, leaving gradient judgments, semantic-pragmatic interactions, and multi-sentence structures underexplored.
Open theoretical questions about minimal inductive bias, architectural interventions, and relation to semantic grounding.
future_direction: Extend SSI to token-level activations or attention maps.
Explore gradient judgments, semantic-pragmatic interactions, and multi-sentence structures beyond binary acceptability.
Investigate the minimal inductive bias or data regime required for syntactic specialization, architectural interventions, and how syntactic development relates to semantic grounding.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been found to develop surprising internal specializations: Individual neurons, attention heads, and circuits become selectively sensitive to syntactic structure, reflecting patterns observed in the human brain. While this specialization is well-documented, how it emerges during training and what influences its development remains largely unknown. In this work, we tap into the black box of specialization by tracking its formation over time. By quantifying internal syntactic consistency across minimal pairs from various syntactic phenomena, we identify a clear developmental trajectory: Syntactic sensitivity emerges gradually, concentrates in specific layers, and exhibits a 'critical period' of rapid internal specialization. This process is consistent across architectures and initialization parameters (e.g., random seeds), and is influenced by model scale and training data. We therefore reveal not only where syntax arises in LLMs but also how some models internalize it during training. To support future research, we will release the code, models, and training checkpoints upon acceptance.

papers.title: Mechanisms vs. Outcomes: Probing for Syntax Fails to Explain Performance on Targeted Syntactic Evaluations
papers.research_question: Do probing accuracies, measured by dependency tree attachment scores of syntactic probes, effectively predict a model’s downstream performance on targeted syntactic evaluations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that syntactic features extracted via probing fail to predict outcomes of targeted syntax evaluations, highlighting a disconnect between latent syntactic representations and observable syntactic behaviors.
papers.conclusion: Probing fails to reliably extract the latent syntactic knowledge within models that correlates with minimal pair accuracy, arguing for targeted evaluations like BLiMP as the gold standard for assessing syntactic competence.
papers.key_findings:
No significant regression fit between probing accuracy and overall BLiMP minimal pair accuracy across 32 models.
Only anaphor agreement shows a significant correlation, but a non-syntactic control probe yields a similar fit, suggesting it is spurious.
Probe recovery of critical syntactic edges (e.g., subject-verb) only weakly aligns with minimal pair outcomes (40–60% match rate).
In over 85% of BLiMP paradigms, UUAS score distributions for correct and incorrect minimal pairs substantially overlap.
Control probes trained on non-syntactic information can also predict some syntactic benchmark performance, indicating that probing results may not be attributable solely to syntactic representations.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation only uses English grammatical benchmarks.
Probe architectures are limited to linear and bilinear probes; other architectures could yield different results.
Models are limited to up to 8B parameters due to compute constraints.
future_direction: Extending the work to multilingual benchmarks (e.g., MultiBLiMP, TurBLiMP).
Exploring other probe architectures and syntactic probing tasks.
Investigating causal relationships between probed representations and model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit a robust mastery of syntax when processing and generating text. While this suggests internalized understanding of hierarchical syntax and dependency relations, the precise mechanism by which they represent syntactic structure is an open area within interpretability research. Probing provides one way to identify the mechanism of syntax being linearly encoded in activations, however, no comprehensive study has yet established whether a model's probing accuracy reliably predicts its downstream syntactic performance. Adopting a "mechanisms vs. outcomes" framework, we evaluate 32 open-weight transformer models and find that syntactic features extracted via probing fail to predict outcomes of targeted syntax evaluations across English linguistic phenomena. Our results highlight a substantial disconnect between latent syntactic representations found via probing and observable syntactic behaviors in downstream tasks.

papers.title: Sudden Drops in the Loss: Syntax Acquisition, Phase Transitions, and Simplicity Bias in MLMs
papers.research_question: How does syntactic attention structure (SAS) emerge during training of masked language models, and what is its causal role in the development of grammatical capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that syntactic attention structure (SAS) emerges abruptly during training and is necessary for grammatical capabilities; briefly suppressing SAS early in training can improve model quality by allowing an alternative strategy to emerge.
papers.conclusion: Developmental analysis of training dynamics is crucial for understanding model behavior, and SAS represents a simplicity bias that can be manipulated to improve training.
papers.key_findings:
SAS emerges abruptly during training in a phase transition called the structure onset.
The structure onset precedes and is necessary for the capabilities onset, which marks improvements in grammatical capabilities.
Suppressing SAS throughout training prevents the development of grammatical capabilities.
Briefly suppressing SAS early in training improves model quality and accelerates convergence.
There exists an alternative strategy that competes with SAS, and suppressing SAS allows this alternative strategy to emerge earlier.
papers.abstract: Most interpretability research in NLP focuses on understanding the behavior and features of a fully trained model. However, certain insights into model behavior may only be accessible by observing the trajectory of the training process. We present a case study of syntax acquisition in masked language models (MLMs) that demonstrates how analyzing the evolution of interpretable artifacts throughout training deepens our understanding of emergent behavior. In particular, we study Syntactic Attention Structure (SAS), a naturally emerging property of MLMs wherein specific Transformer heads tend to focus on specific syntactic relations. We identify a brief window in pretraining when models abruptly acquire SAS, concurrent with a steep drop in loss. This breakthrough precipitates the subsequent acquisition of linguistic capabilities. We then examine the causal role of SAS by manipulating SAS during training, and demonstrate that SAS is necessary for the development of grammatical capabilities. We further find that SAS competes with other beneficial traits during training, and that briefly suppressing SAS improves model quality. These findings offer an interpretation of a real-world example of both simplicity bias and breakthrough training dynamics.

papers.title: Cognitive Mirrors: Exploring the Diverse Functional Roles of Attention Heads in LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in large language models specialize for different cognitive functions during complex reasoning tasks, and what are their properties and roles?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel interpretability framework and the CogQA dataset to analyze attention heads in LLMs, revealing that cognitive heads are sparse, functionally specialized, and hierarchically organized, and are crucial for reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a deeper understanding of LLM reasoning and suggests implications for model design, training, and fine-tuning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads exhibit functional specialization for specific cognitive functions (cognitive heads) and are sparse (only a small subset of heads are important for each function).
Cognitive heads are universal across different LLM architectures and model sizes.
Cognitive heads show layered functional organization, with different functions localizing to different layers (e.g., retrieval in middle layers, math in higher layers).
Cognitive heads exhibit functional clustering and hierarchical structure, where lower-level functions (e.g., retrieval) support higher-level reasoning.
Removing cognitive heads degrades performance on corresponding functions, while enhancing them improves reasoning accuracy, demonstrating their causal importance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance in a variety of tasks, but remain largely opaque in terms of their internal mechanisms. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial to improve their reasoning abilities. Drawing inspiration from the interplay between neural processes and human cognition, we propose a novel interpretability framework to systematically analyze the roles and behaviors of attention heads, which are key components of LLMs. We introduce CogQA, a dataset that decomposes complex questions into step-by-step subquestions with a chain-of-thought design, each associated with specific cognitive functions such as retrieval or logical reasoning. By applying a multi-class probing method, we identify the attention heads responsible for these functions. Our analysis across multiple LLM families reveals that attention heads exhibit functional specialization, characterized as cognitive heads. These cognitive heads exhibit several key properties: they are universally sparse, vary in number and distribution across different cognitive functions, and display interactive and hierarchical structures. We further show that cognitive heads play a vital role in reasoning tasks - removing them leads to performance degradation, while augmenting them enhances reasoning accuracy. These insights offer a deeper understanding of LLM reasoning and suggest important implications for model design, training, and fine-tuning strategies.

papers.title: Compositional generalization in a deep seq2seq model by separating syntax and semantics
papers.research_question: Does separating syntactic and semantic processing in a neural machine translation model improve compositional generalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel seq2seq model, Syntactic Attention, which separates syntactic and semantic processing streams. This architectural constraint substantially improves compositional generalization on the SCAN dataset without hand-engineered features or additional supervision.
papers.conclusion: Separating syntactic and semantic information processing in neural networks encourages systematic, compositional generalization, drawing a conceptual link to hypothesized brain mechanisms and suggesting a useful heuristic for AI.
papers.key_findings:
The Syntactic Attention model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the SCAN dataset's add-jump split, with a median accuracy of 91.0%, a significant improvement over prior models.
The model's performance is highly variable across random initializations on the add-jump split, indicating sensitivity to how the novel verb 'jump' is encoded.
Ablation experiments show that allowing sequential information into the semantic stream ('sequential semantics') degrades compositional generalization, supporting the separation hypothesis.
The model generalizes well from very few examples of a novel verb, achieving near-perfect accuracy with just two training examples containing 'jump'.
The model fails on some SCAN template splits (e.g., 'Primitive opposite right'), indicating limitations in generalizing based on symmetry when training data is skewed.
papers.limitation:
The model's performance on the add-jump split is highly variable and skewed across different random initializations, with some runs failing catastrophically.
The separation between syntax and semantics in the brain is likely not as strict as implemented in the model, suggesting the principle may be more of a useful heuristic than a biological fact.
future_direction: Future research should investigate the factors causing performance variability on tasks like the add-jump split and whether other priors or regularization techniques can overcome it.
The principle of separating syntax and semantics may be a useful heuristic in other natural language processing tasks and other systematic or compositional generalization tasks.
papers.abstract: Standard methods in deep learning for natural language processing fail to capture the compositional structure of human language that allows for systematic generalization outside of the training distribution. However, human learners readily generalize in this way, e.g. by applying known grammatical rules to novel words. Inspired by work in neuroscience suggesting separate brain systems for syntactic and semantic processing, we implement a modification to standard approaches in neural machine translation, imposing an analogous separation. The novel model, which we call Syntactic Attention, substantially outperforms standard methods in deep learning on the SCAN dataset, a compositional generalization task, without any hand-engineered features or additional supervision. Our work suggests that separating syntactic from semantic learning may be a useful heuristic for capturing compositional structure.

papers.title: Toward Mechanistic Explanation of Deductive Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does a small language model solve a deductive reasoning task, and what internal mechanisms (e.g., induction heads) are involved in implementing the logical inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a small language model can learn deductive reasoning by implementing rule-based circuits, with induction heads playing a central role, and introduces a truncated pseudoinverse technique for decoding query, key, and value information.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a tiny LM can learn deductive reasoning by implementing symbolic rule-based circuits, with induction heads being a fundamental component, and suggests that induction heads may also be central in more complex logical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A simplified NanoGPT model trained with Chain-of-Thought can learn deductive reasoning rules and generalize to unseen examples.
Induction heads are crucial for implementing rule completion and rule chaining steps in the logical inference.
The model learns the underlying inference rules rather than memorizing patterns.
A single attention head can host multiple induction heads and other circuits, simplifying post-hoc explanation.
Training without Chain-of-Thought leads to memorization and poor generalization, indicating the importance of CoT for learning rules.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability techniques used (e.g., residual stream decoding and truncated pseudoinverse) are not 100% precise and may fail to decode the expected tokens.
The deductive reasoning task is simple and does not reflect the complexity of real-world logical reasoning.
future_direction: Investigating whether one-layer circuits resembling induction heads can be created by modifying the attention mechanism to decouple key and value positions.
Exploring the role of induction heads in solving more complex logical problems with larger language models.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have demonstrated relevant capabilities in solving problems that require logical reasoning; however, the corresponding internal mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we show that a small language model can solve a deductive reasoning task by learning the underlying rules (rather than operating as a statistical learner). A low-level explanation of its internal representations and computational circuits is then provided. Our findings reveal that induction heads play a central role in the implementation of the rule completion and rule chaining steps involved in the logical inference required by the task.

papers.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
papers.research_question: Do induction heads constitute the mechanism for the majority of in-context learning in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Presents evidence that induction heads, a type of attention head circuit, are the primary mechanism for in-context learning in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: Induction heads likely explain a large fraction of in-context learning in transformers, with strong evidence in small models and correlational evidence in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads form abruptly during a phase change in training, coinciding with a sharp increase in in-context learning ability.
Altering the transformer architecture to shift the formation of induction heads also shifts the improvement in in-context learning.
Ablating induction heads in small models greatly reduces in-context learning.
Induction heads exhibit general in-context learning behaviors beyond literal copying, such as translation.
The mechanism of induction heads in small models suggests how they could be repurposed for general in-context learning.
papers.limitation: Evidence for large models is correlational and could be confounded by other factors.
future_direction: Establish the claim more firmly with additional evidence
Study the phase change in more detail
papers.abstract: "Induction heads" are attention heads that implement a simple algorithm to complete token sequences like [A][B] ... [A] -> [B]. In this work, we present preliminary and indirect evidence for a hypothesis that induction heads might constitute the mechanism for the majority of all "in-context learning" in large transformer models (i.e. decreasing loss at increasing token indices). We find that induction heads develop at precisely the same point as a sudden sharp increase in in-context learning ability, visible as a bump in the training loss. We present six complementary lines of evidence, arguing that induction heads may be the mechanistic source of general in-context learning in transformer models of any size. For small attention-only models, we present strong, causal evidence; for larger models with MLPs, we present correlational evidence.

papers.title: A Theory of Emergent In-Context Learning as Implicit Structure Induction
papers.research_question: When and how does in-context learning (ICL) emerge from generic next-token prediction in language models? The paper investigates the conditions under which ICL capabilities arise from the recombination of compositional operations found in natural language pretraining data.
papers.core_contribution: Provides a theoretical framework showing that in-context learning emerges from next-token prediction when the pretraining distribution has sufficient compositional structure, and validates this with experiments showing ICL emergence in scaled transformer LMs.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning in language models arises from the recombination of compositional structure found in linguistic data, and the paper provides a theoretical and empirical step towards understanding this emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
In-context learning emerges when scaling model parameters and data on compositionally structured pretraining distributions.
Prompting models to output intermediate steps (chain-of-thought) provides a theoretical and empirical benefit over direct prompting.
The success of ICL depends on the complexity of the task's compositional description and the iteration complexity of the pretraining data structure.
Probing experiments indicate that in-context learning is supported by the model learning a representation of the input's compositional structure.
The theoretical bounds are independent of the size of the object universe |Ω|, and empirical performance can even improve with larger |Ω|.
papers.limitation: The theoretical analysis considers an idealized predictor with infinite data and capacity, which may not fully capture the complexities of real-world finite transformer models.
future_direction: Exploring more complex compositional structures and their learnability.
Investigating the application of the theory to real-world natural language data and models.
Extending the analysis to longer chains of reasoning and more complex task compositions.
papers.abstract: Scaling large language models (LLMs) leads to an emergent capacity to learn in-context from example demonstrations. Despite progress, theoretical understanding of this phenomenon remains limited. We argue that in-context learning relies on recombination of compositional operations found in natural language data. We derive an information-theoretic bound showing how in-context learning abilities arise from generic next-token prediction when the pretraining distribution has sufficient amounts of compositional structure, under linguistically motivated assumptions. A second bound provides a theoretical justification for the empirical success of prompting LLMs to output intermediate steps towards an answer. To validate theoretical predictions, we introduce a controlled setup for inducing in-context learning; unlike previous approaches, it accounts for the compositional nature of language. Trained transformers can perform in-context learning for a range of tasks, in a manner consistent with the theoretical results. Mirroring real-world LLMs in a miniature setup, in-context learning emerges when scaling parameters and data, and models perform better when prompted to output intermediate steps. Probing shows that in-context learning is supported by a representation of the input's compositional structure. Taken together, these results provide a step towards theoretical understanding of emergent behavior in large language models.

papers.title: Syntactic Perturbations Reveal Representational Correlates of Hierarchical Phrase Structure in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: What aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by pretrained language model representations, and how are they built along the layers of the network?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that input perturbations reveal how transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, and that such perturbations are a useful analysis tool for interpreting deep language models.
papers.conclusion: Transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, and attention changes partially explain this sensitivity.
papers.key_findings:
Representations are more distorted by shuffling small n-grams in early layers and by large n-grams in later layers, indicating increasing context scale along layers.
Swapping phrases causes less distortion than swapping non-phrases, indicating sensitivity to phrase structure.
Swapping adjacent words across phrase boundaries causes more distortion than within boundaries, and distortion increases with syntactic distance, especially in deeper layers.
Attention changes partially explain the sensitivity to syntactic distance.
The distortion metric correlates with impairment of syntactic probes (POS, grandparent tags, tree distance).
future_direction: Developing a formal theory of efficient hierarchical data representations in distributed features.
Searching for causal connection between attention structure, representational geometry, and model performance.
Applying perturbation analyses to models trained on shuffled data or models with explicit syntax.
papers.abstract: While vector-based language representations from pretrained language models have set a new standard for many NLP tasks, there is not yet a complete accounting of their inner workings. In particular, it is not entirely clear what aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by these representations, nor how (if at all) they are built along the stacked layers of the network. In this paper, we aim to address such questions with a general class of interventional, input perturbation-based analyses of representations from pretrained language models. Importing from computational and cognitive neuroscience the notion of representational invariance, we perform a series of probes designed to test the sensitivity of these representations to several kinds of structure in sentences. Each probe involves swapping words in a sentence and comparing the representations from perturbed sentences against the original. We experiment with three different perturbations: (1) random permutations of n-grams of varying width, to test the scale at which a representation is sensitive to word position; (2) swapping of two spans which do or do not form a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to global phrase structure; and (3) swapping of two adjacent words which do or do not break apart a syntactic phrase, to test sensitivity to local phrase structure. Results from these probes collectively suggest that Transformers build sensitivity to larger parts of the sentence along their layers, and that hierarchical phrase structure plays a role in this process. More broadly, our results also indicate that structured input perturbations widens the scope of analyses that can be performed on often-opaque deep learning systems, and can serve as a complement to existing tools (such as supervised linear probes) for interpreting complex black-box models. 1

papers.title: How to Plant Trees in Language Models: Data and Architectural Effects on the Emergence of Syntactic Inductive Biases
papers.research_question: What architectural features and pre-training data properties contribute to the emergence of hierarchical syntactic inductive biases in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that model depth is more critical than width for hierarchical syntactic generalization in Transformers, and that pre-training on simpler language like child-directed speech induces such biases with orders-of-magnitude less data than web text.
papers.conclusion: The study finds that model depth is more important than other architectural components for hierarchical generalization, and that simpler pre-training data leads to faster acquisition of syntactic inductive biases, suggesting Transformers may be more data-efficient in cognitively plausible settings.
papers.key_findings:
Model depth has a greater impact on hierarchical generalization than model width or number of parameters alone.
Pre-training on child-directed speech enables hierarchical generalization with far less data (5M words) compared to Wikipedia or web text (100M-1B words).
The number of parameters does not monotonically predict syntactic generalization accuracy.
Syntactic generalization accuracy correlates with language modeling performance and downstream task performance.
Simpler language, such as Simple Wikipedia, also induces hierarchical biases more efficiently than standard Wikipedia.
papers.limitation:
Findings may not generalize to other types of encoder-decoder models, encoder-only, or decoder-only models.
Analysis is based only on English and two syntactic transformations, which may not cover all linguistic phenomena.
future_direction: Using methods to measure the tree-likeness of Transformer representations during pre-training.
Disentangling the effects of lexical and syntactic complexity in pre-training data.
Exploring a two-phase 'starting small' pre-training approach.
papers.abstract: Accurate syntactic representations are essential for robust generalization in natural language. Recent work has found that pre-training can teach language models to rely on hierarchical syntactic features - as opposed to incorrect linear features - when performing tasks after fine-tuning. We test what aspects of pre-training are important for endowing encoder-decoder Transformers with an inductive bias that favors hierarchical syntactic generalizations. We focus on architectural features (depth, width, and number of parameters), as well as the genre and size of the pre-training corpus, diagnosing inductive biases using two syntactic transformation tasks: question formation and passivization, both in English. We find that the number of parameters alone does not explain hierarchical generalization: model depth plays greater role than model width. We also find that pre-training on simpler language, such as child-directed speech, induces a hierarchical bias using an order-of-magnitude less data than pre-training on more typical datasets based on web text or Wikipedia; this suggests that in cognitively plausible language acquisition settings, neural language models may be more data-efficient than previously thought.

papers.title: Contextualize-then-Aggregate: Circuits for In-Context Learning in Gemma-2 2B
papers.research_question: What mechanism assembles task information from the individual examples in a few-shot prompt during in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a two-step 'contextualize-then-aggregate' circuit for in-context learning in Gemma-2, where lower layers contextualize individual few-shot examples and higher layers aggregate this information to predict the next token.
papers.conclusion: The paper establishes a two-stage procedure for in-context learning where the model contextualizes representations of individual few-shot examples before aggregating them to prepare the next-token prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The model uses a two-step strategy: contextualization of individual few-shot examples in lower layers, followed by aggregation of task information in higher layers.
The aggregation step alone is insufficient for full performance on some tasks; contextualization is crucial, especially with ambiguous examples.
The identified circuits recover at least 90% of the full model's performance across five ICL tasks.
The information transported differs by edge type: aggregation edges generally move task information, while contextualization edges move information about input/output spaces.
The importance and specific edges of the contextualization subcircuit vary between tasks.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is limited to five tasks and one model family (Gemma-2).
Circuit discovery relies on patching, which requires careful design of counterfactual inputs.
The study does not provide a full interpretation of all individual components in the model.
future_direction: Extend the approach to more tasks and models.
Investigate the role of contextualization in other settings, such as linear regression tasks.
Provide a more fine-grained interpretation of individual components.
papers.abstract: In-Context Learning (ICL) is an intriguing ability of large language models (LLMs). Despite a substantial amount of work on its behavioral aspects and how it emerges in miniature setups, it remains unclear which mechanism assembles task information from the individual examples in a fewshot prompt. We use causal interventions to identify information flow in Gemma-2 2B for five naturalistic ICL tasks. We find that the model infers task information using a two-step strategy we call contextualize-then-aggregate: In the lower layers, the model builds up representations of individual fewshot examples, which are contextualized by preceding examples through connections between fewshot input and output tokens across the sequence. In the higher layers, these representations are aggregated to identify the task and prepare prediction of the next output. The importance of the contextualization step differs between tasks, and it may become more important in the presence of ambiguous examples. Overall, by providing rigorous causal analysis, our results shed light on the mechanisms through which ICL happens in language models.

papers.title: Inferring the nature of linguistic computations in the brain
papers.research_question: How can we infer the nature of linguistic computations from neural data, and what are the pitfalls in interpreting such data and models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that neural data alone is insufficient to infer the computational mechanisms of sentence processing, and that models must be evaluated based on cognitive, neural, and linguistic principles to be explanatory.
papers.conclusion: Computational modeling is vital for understanding sentence processing, but models must compute linguistically-sufficient representations via explicit cognitive operations and stay faithful to neurophysiological principles, and should not be judged solely on predictive power.
papers.key_findings:
The presence of a 1-2-4 Hz pattern in neural data does not necessarily imply hierarchical processing; it can also arise from associative models.
Artificial neural networks can produce the 1-2-4 Hz pattern without explicit sentence structure, but this does not rule out hierarchical processing in the brain.
Predictive power of a model is not the sole criterion for explaining brain function; models must also be faithful to cognitive and neural principles.
The amount of training data used in ANNs may not reflect the brain's learning environment, and rule-based models might be more explanatory in some cases.
Statistical models are not necessarily more parsimonious than hierarchical models, as they may require extensive training and latent syntactic information.
future_direction: Using naturalistic paradigms to study language processing
Integrating multiple data sources (e.g., EEG, fMRI) to test models
Developing models that are explicit about cognitive operations and neurophysiological implementation
papers.abstract: Sentences contain structure that determines their meaning beyond that of individual words. An influential study by Ding and colleagues (2016) used frequency tagging of phrases and sentences to show that the human brain is sensitive to structure by finding peaks of neural power at the rate at which structures were presented. Since then, there has been a rich debate on how to best explain this pattern of results with profound impact on the language sciences. Models that use hierarchical structure building, as well as models based on associative sequence processing, can predict the neural response, creating an inferential impasse as to which class of models explains the nature of the linguistic computations reflected in the neural readout. In the current manuscript, we discuss pitfalls and common fallacies seen in the conclusions drawn in the literature illustrated by various simulations. We conclude that inferring the neural operations of sentence processing based on these neural data, and any like it, alone, is insufficient. We discuss how to best evaluate models and how to approach the modeling of neural readouts to sentence processing in a manner that remains faithful to cognitive, neural, and linguistic principles.

papers.title: Understanding Syntax in Large Language Models: Successes and Limitations
papers.research_question: How accurately can LLMs handle published examples of complex syntactic phenomena, as described in linguistic theories?
papers.core_contribution: This study evaluates the syntactic competence of LLMs, finding that while they handle simple constructions well, they struggle with complex hierarchical dependencies, highlighting the need for integrating explicit syntactic principles.
papers.conclusion: LLMs demonstrate competence in simple syntax but struggle with complex structures, indicating a gap between surface fluency and deep syntactic competence, necessitating hybrid approaches for improvement.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit high success rates for simple relative clauses and basic wh-movement, but performance declines with increased complexity.
Center-embedding poses significant challenges, with success rates dropping to around 50% for deeply embedded structures.
Errors include truncation of sentences, unresolved syntactic dependencies, and semantic incoherence in complex cases.
LLMs rely on surface-level pattern recognition rather than deep generative syntactic principles.
The limitations suggest that current LLMs lack robust internal representations of hierarchical syntax.
papers.limitation:
The analysis relied exclusively on examples from English linguistic literature, not capturing syntactic diversity across languages.
The evaluation focused only on relative clauses, wh-movement, and center-embedding, without exploring broader syntactic constructs.
The study was limited to publicly available LLMs like GPT-4 and BERT, without considering effects of model size, architecture, or training data.
The evaluation did not delve into underlying representations or mechanisms of the models.
future_direction: Integrating explicit syntactic theory into neural architectures, such as the Minimalist Program or dependency grammar.
Conducting cross-linguistic comparisons to evaluate LLMs' syntactic competence across different languages.
Designing more linguistically focused benchmarks based on theoretical constructs like syntactic islands or scope ambiguity.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to process complex syntactic phenomena, including relative clauses, wh-movement, and center- embedding. By analyzing examples derived from linguistic literature, the study highlights both the strengths and limitations of LLMs in handling syntax. The results reveal that while LLMs exhibit competence in simpler syntactic constructions, they struggle with deeper hierarchical dependencies and abstract syntactic constraints. The study underscores the need for integrating explicit syntactic principles into LLM architectures to bridge the gap between surface-level fluency and generative linguistic competence.

papers.title: Ungrammatical Influences: Evidence for Dynamical Language Processing
papers.research_question: Do ungrammatical influences exist in human sentence processing? Specifically, are readers temporarily distracted by coherent but grammatically incompatible local structures during parsing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence from a connectionist model and human reading experiments that ungrammatical local structures can influence parsing, supporting a dynamical, self-organizing approach to language processing.
papers.conclusion: Ungrammatical influences exist in human sentence processing, and dynamical, self-organizing models like connectionist networks can account for these effects, pointing towards parallel processing solutions to parsing tractability.
papers.key_findings:
A Simple Recurrent Network model shows higher error (Kullback-Leibler Divergence) on sentences containing irrelevant local coherences (e.g., noun-noun compounds) that are grammatically incompatible with the global structure.
Human reading times are slower for sentences containing such ungrammatical local coherences (Experiment 1), indicating distraction by grammatically ruled-out interpretations.
A stronger slowing effect is found for reduced relative clauses with homophonous verbs compared to non-homophonous verbs (Experiment 2), showing the effect extends beyond lexical compounds.
The results suggest that parsing involves competition among local coherences via dynamical feedback, rather than deductive elimination of parses based on top-down constraints.
The connectionist model's behavior aligns with human data, indicating that dynamical, self-organizing mechanisms may address tractability problems in parsing.
papers.limitation:
The effect in the network simulation was somewhat unstable with longer training on the same materials and sometimes reversed itself.
Experiment 1 results could be explained by lexical automaticity (activation of compound senses in the lexicon) rather than syntactic parsing interference, though Experiment 2 addresses this.
future_direction: Further exploration of dynamical parsing models that use feedback and self-organization to handle incoherent structure representation.
Incorporating the problem of incoherent structure representation into the theory of grammar.
papers.abstract: Ungrammatical Inuences: Evidence for Dynamical Language Processing Whitney Tabor tabor@uconnvm.uconn.edu Bruno Galantucci Bruno.Galantucci@uconn.edu Department of Psychology University of Connecticut Storrs, CT 06269 USA Abstract A distinguishing feature of self-organizing models of cog- nitive structure is that they permit incompatible struc- tures to coexist at least temporarily. Here we report on a connectionist model of natural language process- ing which appears to temporarily construct incoherent structures. We then describe two reading-time studies which reveal people exhibiting the same tendency. In particular, both networks and people show sensitivity to the irrelevant structural interpretations of the under- lined phrases in (1) and (2). (1) We did not think the company would re truck drivers without consulting the union rst. (2) The manager watched the waiter served pea soup by the trainee. This kind of sensitivity is absent in parsing models which treat grammatical constraints as absolute because such models lack a principled method of generating incoher- ent parses. Connectionist networks make the right pre- dictions by using feedback and self-organization. Our results push in the direction of seeking a solution to the tractability problems of parsing by using dynamical mechanisms in a parallel architecture. Introduction Current sentence-processing research tends to focus on ambiguity-related processing in sentences like (1) { (3): (1) The mechanic maintained the truck was working beautifully. (2) The cop arrested by the detective was chagrined. (3) The cook stirred the soup with the tomatoes. Each of these sentences has a structural ambiguity which is resolved on the basis of structural or pragmatic infor- mation when the underlined words arrive. Reading time and eye tracking studies show that when biases favor the wrong interpretation initially, readers tend to slow down and/or make regressions in the disambiguating re- gion, which suggests that they either choose the wrong parse initially or are biased toward it (see Frazier, 1988; Tanenhaus & Trueswell, 1995). Such phenomena accord well with a model of sen- tence processing which assumes people construct phrase- structure parses incrementally based on the input up to the current point in time. On this view, the slow-down in the disambiguating region is due either to extra time Figure 1: The Zollner illusion. spent on revising an incorrect parse, or to extra time spent on revising the weighting assigned to dierent pos- sible parses maintained in parallel. Focusing for a moment on cognitive processes outside of sentence processing, there is a good deal of evidence that people are reliably vulnerable to certain adverse inuences when interpreting complex stimuli. In the Zollner illusion (Held, 1971|Figure 1), lines on a page appear to be nonparallel even though retinal and depth of eld information indicate parallelism. Similarly, in the Stroop eect (Stroop, 1966), a decision is supposed to have been made ahead of time to interpret the stimulus along one particular dimension of contrast (e.g. color), and yet when the stimulus is presented, people are often led astray by irrelevant verbal information. These cases are dierent from the classic sentence pro- cessing examples listed in (1) through (3) in that they show people temporarily failing to rule out an interpre- tation that could be ruled out absolutely, given the in- formation at hand. What would be the analogous cases in sentence processing? Denition of Ungrammatical Inuences There is a class of sentences in which one parse of a word sequence can be completely ruled out on grammatical grounds and yet (we hypothesize) people are inuenced by it anyway. The following are examples of such hy- pothesized \Ungrammatical Inuences : (4) a. They won't re truck drivers on Sunday. b. They won't hire truck drivers on Sunday.

papers.title: Large Language Models are In-Context Semantic Reasoners rather than Symbolic Reasoners
papers.research_question: Are LLMs good in-context reasoners without semantics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that semantics are vital for LLMs' in-context reasoning; they perform well when semantics align with commonsense but struggle with symbolic or counter-commonsense reasoning, relying on superficial semantic connections rather than formal symbolic reasoning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs rely heavily on learned semantics for in-context reasoning, creating strong token connections that compose a superficial logical chain, rather than performing formal symbolic reasoning like humans.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs perform significantly better on reasoning tasks when semantics are consistent with commonsense compared to when semantics are decoupled (symbolic setting).
LLMs struggle to solve symbolic or counter-commonsense reasoning tasks by leveraging in-context new knowledge.
Semantic knowledge is easier for LLMs to memorize than symbolic knowledge, but updating semantic knowledge has a higher forgetting ratio due to stronger correlations.
LLMs' reasoning performance is inferior to logic-based symbolic methods across all tested reasoning tasks (deduction, induction, abduction).
The length of the in-context information impacts reasoning performance, with shorter contexts leading to better results.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to specific datasets (Symbolic Tree, ProofWriter) and models (ChatGPT, GPT-4, LLaMA-7B).
Long-context reasoning is challenging for LLMs, as they struggle to select relevant information from excessively long prompts.
future_direction: Combining LLMs with non-parametric knowledge bases (e.g., graph databases) for more efficient and accurate knowledge updating and reasoning.
Further research on neural-symbolic AI systems to leverage the strengths of both neural and symbolic approaches.
Investigating the internal mechanisms of LLMs to better understand how they utilize semantics for reasoning.
papers.abstract: The emergent few-shot reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) have excited the natural language and machine learning community over recent years. Despite of numerous successful applications, the underlying mechanism of such in-context capabilities still remains unclear. In this work, we hypothesize that the learned \textit{semantics} of language tokens do the most heavy lifting during the reasoning process. Different from human's symbolic reasoning process, the semantic representations of LLMs could create strong connections among tokens, thus composing a superficial logical chain. To test our hypothesis, we decouple semantics from the language reasoning process and evaluate three kinds of reasoning abilities, i.e., deduction, induction and abduction. Our findings reveal that semantics play a vital role in LLMs' in-context reasoning -- LLMs perform significantly better when semantics are consistent with commonsense but struggle to solve symbolic or counter-commonsense reasoning tasks by leveraging in-context new knowledge. The surprising observations question whether modern LLMs have mastered the inductive, deductive and abductive reasoning abilities as in human intelligence, and motivate research on unveiling the magic existing within the black-box LLMs. On the whole, our analysis provides a novel perspective on the role of semantics in developing and evaluating language models' reasoning abilities. Code is available at {\url{https://github.com/XiaojuanTang/ICSR}}.

papers.title: Localizing Task Recognition and Task Learning in In-Context Learning via Attention Head Analysis
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in large language models mechanistically implement in-context learning, specifically the components of task recognition and task learning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Task Subspace Logit Attribution (TSLA) to identify attention heads specialized in task recognition and task learning, providing a unified mechanistic account of in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The TSLA framework successfully localizes TR and TL components to specific attention heads, providing a unified mechanistic explanation of in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
TR heads and induction heads are highly overlapping and correlated, indicating that induction heads primarily contribute to task recognition.
TR heads attend more to demonstration labels, while TL heads attend more to query tokens.
Ablating TR heads reduces both accuracy and TR ratio, while ablating TL heads reduces accuracy but not TR ratio.
TR heads align hidden states with the task subspace, while TL heads rotate hidden states within the subspace toward the correct label.
The identified TR heads are consistent across tasks, while TL heads are more task-specific.
papers.abstract: We investigate the mechanistic underpinnings of in-context learning (ICL) in large language models by reconciling two dominant perspectives: the component-level analysis of attention heads and the holistic decomposition of ICL into Task Recognition (TR) and Task Learning (TL). We propose a novel framework based on Task Subspace Logit Attribution (TSLA) to identify attention heads specialized in TR and TL, and demonstrate their distinct yet complementary roles. Through correlation analysis, ablation studies, and input perturbations, we show that the identified TR and TL heads independently and effectively capture the TR and TL components of ICL. Using steering experiments with geometric analysis of hidden states, we reveal that TR heads promote task recognition by aligning hidden states with the task subspace, while TL heads rotate hidden states within the subspace toward the correct label to facilitate prediction. We further show how previous findings on ICL mechanisms, including induction heads and task vectors, can be reconciled with our attention-head-level analysis of the TR-TL decomposition. Our framework thus provides a unified and interpretable account of how large language models execute ICL across diverse tasks and settings.

papers.title: Structural Supervision Improves Few-Shot Learning and Syntactic Generalization in Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the ability of neural language models to make syntactic generalizations from minimal exposure, and how does structural supervision affect learning outcomes and syntactic invariance?
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models can learn syntactic generalizations from few examples, and explicit structural supervision improves both few-shot learning and syntactic invariance across transformations.
papers.conclusion: Neural language models are capable of inducing syntactic features from minimal exposure and show some invariance to syntactic transformations, with structural supervision enhancing these abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Neural models show robust few-shot learning for nominal number and verbal argument structure after minimal exposure.
Structurally supervised models (ActionLSTM and RNNG) outperform the LSTM model in most syntactic generalization tests.
Models demonstrate syntactic invariance by transferring generalizations learned in base contexts to transformed contexts.
There is a singular bias for nouns and a transitive bias for verbs in few-shot learning, with models assuming default categories when evidence is sparse.
Accuracy often improves with increased exposure for some tests, particularly for structurally supervised models.
papers.limitation: The small training data size poses limitations and suggests the need for scaling to larger datasets for better generalization.
future_direction: Scaling the carefully-controlled methods to larger data settings.
papers.abstract: Humans can learn structural properties about a word from minimal experience, and deploy their learned syntactic representations uniformly in different grammatical contexts. We assess the ability of modern neural language models to reproduce this behavior in English and evaluate the effect of structural supervision on learning outcomes. First, we assess few-shot learning capabilities by developing controlled experiments that probe models' syntactic nominal number and verbal argument structure generalizations for tokens seen as few as two times during training. Second, we assess invariance properties of learned representation: the ability of a model to transfer syntactic generalizations from a base context (e.g., a simple declarative active-voice sentence) to a transformed context (e.g., an interrogative sentence). We test four models trained on the same dataset: an n-gram baseline, an LSTM, and two LSTM-variants trained with explicit structural supervision (Dyer et al.,2016; Charniak et al., 2016). We find that in most cases, the neural models are able to induce the proper syntactic generalizations after minimal exposure, often from just two examples during training, and that the two structurally supervised models generalize more accurately than the LSTM model. All neural models are able to leverage information learned in base contexts to drive expectations in transformed contexts, indicating that they have learned some invariance properties of syntax.

papers.title: Reasoning Circuits in Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Syllogistic Inference
papers.research_question: How is content-independent syllogistic reasoning internalized in LMs during pre-training? Are content-independent mechanisms disentangled from world knowledge and belief biases? Does the core reasoning mechanism generalize across syllogistic schemes, model sizes, and architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a sufficient and necessary circuit for syllogistic reasoning involving middle-term suppression, showing that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms that are susceptible to contamination from world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn transferable reasoning mechanisms but such mechanisms are contaminated and suppressed by the world knowledge acquired during pre-training, indicating a lack of generalizable abstract logical primitives.
papers.key_findings:
The circuit for syllogistic reasoning involves a three-stage mechanism: long induction, duplication, suppression, and mover heads.
The circuit is necessary and sufficient for symbolic syllogistic reasoning.
The circuit transfers to non-symbolic arguments but is contaminated by belief biases, with additional attention heads encoding world knowledge.
The circuit generalizes across unconditionally valid syllogistic schemes where models achieve high accuracy.
The suppression mechanism pattern is compatible across different model families and sizes, though with increasing complexity in larger models.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is confined to specific syllogistic reasoning templates and does not consider more complex scenarios.
The experimentation is confined due to the intricate level of granularity and computational complexity required in circuit analysis.
future_direction: Further studies to understand how the discovered symbolic circuit can be effectively disentangled from world knowledge to enable systematic generalization in LMs’ reasoning.
